questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The 'basic structure' doctrine was first propounded by the Supreme Court in:

options.A: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
options.B: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967)
options.C: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
options.D: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)

questions.explanation: A 13-judge Bench in Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The Right to Education was made a Fundamental Right under Article 21A by the:
questions.explanation: The 86th Amendment inserted Article 21A, providing free and compulsory education to children aged six to fourteen years.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which writ is issued to inquire into the legality of a person's claim to a public office?
questions.explanation: Quo warranto ('by what authority') prevents illegal usurpation of a public office.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar describe as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and is itself a Fundamental Right.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: After the 44th Amendment, a Proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within:
questions.explanation: Post the 44th Amendment, approval is required within one month by a special majority of each House.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The Supreme Court held that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable in:

options.A: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
options.B: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
options.C: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.

questions.explanation: Maneka Gandhi linked Articles 14, 19 and 21 and rejected the narrow Gopalan view of Article 21.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: In the Rajya Sabha, one-third of the members retire after every:
questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha is a permanent House; members have a six-year term and one-third retire every second year.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: An amendment affecting the representation of States in Parliament requires, under Article 368, a special majority and:

options.A: Ratification by legislatures of at least one-half of the States
options.B: Ratification by legislatures of at least two-thirds of the States
options.C: Approval through a nationwide referendum by voters
options.D: Prior consent of all the Governors of the States

questions.explanation: Article 368(2) proviso lists federal provisions that need ratification by at least half of the States.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The Directive Principle directing the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens is contained in:
questions.explanation: Article 44 (Part IV) says the State shall endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code throughout India.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) were added to the Constitution on the recommendation of the:
questions.explanation: The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part IVA based on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: Under Article 14, a classification is permissible only if it is based on an intelligible differentia and:

options.A: Bears a rational nexus to the object of the law
options.B: Is expressly enumerated in the Constitution's Preamble
options.C: Applies uniformly to every person within the State
options.D: Receives approval by two-thirds of the legislature

questions.explanation: The 'twin test' of reasonable classification: intelligible differentia + rational nexus to the object of the law.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The Right to Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right under Article 21 by a nine-judge Bench in:

options.A: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (1997)
options.B: Govind v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1975)
options.C: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (1994)
options.D: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)

questions.explanation: Puttaswamy overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they denied privacy as a fundamental right.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: The 'Pure Theory of Law' is associated with:
questions.explanation: Kelsen sought a science of law free from politics, sociology and morality, built around the Grundnorm.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: The theory that law is the command of the sovereign backed by sanction was propounded by:
questions.explanation: Austin's analytical positivism defined law as a command issued by a sovereign to subjects, enforced by sanction.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: The Historical School of jurisprudence is chiefly associated with:
questions.explanation: Savigny argued law grows out of the 'Volksgeist' (spirit of the people) and is not made arbitrarily.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: In Hohfeld's scheme of jural relations, the correlative of a 'right' (claim) is:
questions.explanation: Hohfeld paired right–duty, privilege–no right, power–liability, and immunity–disability.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: The idea of 'law as social engineering' is associated with:
questions.explanation: Pound viewed law as a means of balancing competing social interests.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: The 'rule of recognition' as a secondary rule of law was developed by:
questions.explanation: In The Concept of Law, Hart distinguished primary rules of obligation from secondary rules: recognition, change and adjudication.

questions.subject: Jurisprudence
questions.question: The term 'ratio decidendi' refers to:

options.A: The principle underlying a judicial decision
options.B: The facts stated in the headnote of a report
options.C: The final order of a court on costs
options.D: A passing remark made by a judge in a judgment

questions.explanation: Ratio decidendi is binding precedent; obiter dicta are incidental observations without binding force.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: Under Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a contract is:

options.A: An agreement between two competent parties

questions.explanation: Section 2(h) defines contract as an agreement enforceable by law.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. established that:

options.A: Acceptance must always be communicated in writing
options.B: Advertisements are always mere invitations to treat
options.C: Silence can always amount to valid acceptance by offeree
options.D: A general offer is accepted by performing its terms

questions.explanation: A unilateral offer to the world at large is accepted by conduct; notice of acceptance is not required.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: Under the Indian law, an agreement with a minor is:
questions.explanation: Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) held minor's agreements are absolutely void.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: The doctrine of frustration of contract is codified in which section of the Indian Contract Act?
questions.explanation: Section 56 makes an agreement to do an impossible act void, and covers supervening impossibility (Taylor v. Caldwell principle).

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: The rule on remoteness of damages, reflected in Section 73 of the Contract Act, originated from:
questions.explanation: Hadley v. Baxendale limits recovery to losses arising naturally or within the parties' contemplation.

questions.subject: Law of Contract
questions.question: An agreement in restraint of trade is declared void by:

options.A: Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act
options.B: Section 26 of the Indian Contract Act
options.C: Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
options.D: Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act

questions.explanation: Section 27 voids agreements restraining anyone from a lawful profession, trade or business, subject to the sale-of-goodwill exception.

questions.subject: Sale of Goods
questions.question: The maxim 'caveat emptor' means:
questions.explanation: The buyer must examine goods before purchase; exceptions are carved out in Section 16 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: The rule of strict liability for escape of dangerous things from one's land was laid down in:
questions.explanation: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) imposed liability without proof of negligence for non-natural use of land.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: The doctrine of 'absolute liability', without exceptions, was evolved in India in:

options.A: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
options.B: Vellore Citizens Forum v. Union of India
options.C: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India
options.D: Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster v. Union of India

questions.explanation: The Court held that enterprises engaged in hazardous activity bear absolute liability for harm caused.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: The 'neighbour principle' and modern law of negligence originate from:
questions.explanation: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle established the duty of care in negligence.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: The defence expressed as 'volenti non fit injuria' means:

options.A: The thing speaks for itself, shifting the burden
options.B: Consent to the risk bars any claim for harm
options.C: No man should be a judge in his own cause
options.D: Where there is a right there is a remedy

questions.explanation: Voluntary assumption of risk with full knowledge bars the claim.

questions.subject: Law of Torts
questions.question: Defamation in a permanent form, such as writing or printing, is called:
questions.explanation: Libel is defamation in permanent form; slander is in transient form such as spoken words.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024 and replaced the:
questions.explanation: BNS, BNSS and BSA replaced IPC, CrPC and the Indian Evidence Act respectively.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: Punishment for murder under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is provided in Section:
questions.explanation: Section 101 defines murder, Section 103 prescribes punishment (earlier IPC Section 302); Section 105 deals with culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: The maxim 'actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea' signifies that:

options.A: The accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty
options.B: An act alone is no crime without a guilty mind
options.C: Every legal wrong must have a legal remedy
options.D: Ignorance of law is never an excuse in court

questions.explanation: It captures the requirement of both actus reus and mens rea for criminal liability.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: The offence of sedition under the IPC has been replaced in the BNS by a provision on:

options.A: Acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
options.B: Waging war against any Asiatic power at peace with India
options.C: Promoting enmity between different religious or racial groups
options.D: Unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapons and ammunition

questions.explanation: Section 152 BNS penalises acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India and omits the word 'sedition'.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: Under the BNS, nothing is an offence if done by a child under the age of:
questions.explanation: Absolute immunity applies to a child below seven; between seven and twelve, immunity depends on maturity of understanding.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: An essential ingredient of the offence of theft is that the property must be:
questions.explanation: Theft requires dishonest taking of movable property out of another's possession without consent.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: Which of the following is a new offence in the BNS with no direct counterpart in the IPC?
questions.explanation: Section 111 BNS defines and punishes organised crime, which the IPC did not address.

questions.subject: Criminal Law
questions.question: Which of the following is a newly introduced form of punishment under the BNS?
questions.explanation: Community service has been introduced for certain petty offences; transportation was replaced earlier by imprisonment for life.

questions.subject: Procedural Law
questions.question: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 replaced the:
questions.explanation: BNSS governs criminal procedure with effect from 1 July 2024.

questions.subject: Procedural Law
questions.question: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 provides that civil courts shall have jurisdiction to try:

options.A: All suits, including those of a purely criminal nature
options.B: All civil suits unless expressly or impliedly barred
options.C: Only suits concerning immovable property and its title
options.D: Only suits above a prescribed pecuniary value

questions.explanation: Civil courts have inherent jurisdiction over civil suits, excluding those barred by statute.

questions.subject: Procedural Law
questions.question: The doctrine of res judicata is contained in which section of the CPC?
questions.explanation: Section 11 bars a court from trying a matter already directly and substantially in issue and finally decided; Section 10 deals with res sub judice.

questions.subject: Procedural Law
questions.question: Under the Limitation Act, 1963, the limitation period for a suit for possession of immovable property based on title is:
questions.explanation: Article 65 prescribes twelve years from the time possession becomes adverse to the plaintiff.

questions.subject: Procedural Law
questions.question: A 'Zero FIR' refers to an FIR that:

options.A: Is filed only against persons not yet identified
options.B: Can be lodged at any police station, whatever its area
options.C: Is closed once the investigation yields no result
options.D: Is registered only after a magistrate's order

questions.explanation: The police station receiving the complaint registers it and then transfers it to the police station having jurisdiction.

questions.subject: Procedural Law
questions.question: Anticipatory bail is provided for in which section of the BNSS, 2023?
questions.explanation: Section 482 BNSS corresponds to Section 438 CrPC.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence
questions.question: The Indian Evidence Act, 1872 has been replaced by the:
questions.explanation: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam also gives express recognition to electronic records as documents.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence
questions.question: Admissibility of a dying declaration rests on the maxim:

options.C: Qui facit per alium facit per se

questions.explanation: A person on the verge of death is presumed not to lie.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence
questions.question: A confession made by an accused to a police officer is:
questions.explanation: Section 25 of the Evidence Act (Section 23 BSA) bars proof of confessions made to police officers.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence
questions.question: As a general rule, the burden of proof lies on the person who:

options.A: Denies the claim in the pleadings
options.B: Asserts the affirmative of an issue
options.D: Is called first by the court

questions.explanation: He who asserts must prove; the burden shifts only as provided by law.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The principal judicial organ of the United Nations, the International Court of Justice, has its seat at:
questions.explanation: The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace at The Hague, Netherlands.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The sources of international law are enumerated in which provision?
questions.explanation: Article 38(1) lists treaties, custom, general principles, and judicial decisions and teachings as subsidiary means.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: The principle 'pacta sunt servanda' means:
questions.explanation: It is the foundation of treaty law codified in Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Peremptory norms of general international law from which no derogation is permitted are known as:
questions.explanation: Article 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties makes treaties conflicting with jus cogens void.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: Under UNCLOS, 1982, the breadth of the territorial sea of a coastal State can extend up to:
questions.explanation: The territorial sea is up to 12 nm; the contiguous zone 24 nm; the EEZ 200 nm.

questions.subject: International Law
questions.question: A receiving State may at any time declare a diplomatic agent to be:
questions.explanation: Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961 permits this without giving reasons.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the statutory interval between the first and second motions for divorce by mutual consent is:
questions.explanation: The period is six months, which the Supreme Court has held to be directory and waivable in appropriate cases.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: In Muslim law, 'Mehr' means:

options.A: Property the wife inherits from her parents
options.B: Maintenance payable to the wife after divorce
options.C: A gift made by a father to his daughter at marriage
options.D: A sum the husband must pay the wife on marriage

questions.explanation: Mehr (dower) is an obligation imposed on the husband as a mark of respect to the wife.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: Talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) was declared unconstitutional in:

options.A: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)
options.B: Shamim Ara v. State of U.P. (2002)
options.C: Shah Bano Begum v. Mohd. Ahmed Khan (1985)
options.D: Danial Latifi v. Union of India (2001)

questions.explanation: A majority of the Constitution Bench held the practice to be manifestly arbitrary and violative of Article 14.

questions.subject: Property Law
questions.question: Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, sale of tangible immovable property of value ₹100 and above can be made only by:
questions.explanation: Sale of immovable property of ₹100 or more requires a registered instrument.

questions.subject: Property Law
questions.question: An 'easement' under the Indian Easements Act, 1882 is a right which the owner of land has:

options.A: To lease another's land to third parties
options.B: Over another's land for enjoying his own land
options.C: To collect rent from another person's land

questions.explanation: Easements such as right of way and light and air are rights over land belonging to another, attached to dominant heritage.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that daughters:

options.A: Have no coparcenary rights in joint family property
options.B: Are coparceners by birth, even if the father died before 2005
options.C: Hold rights only in the father's self-acquired property
options.D: Become coparceners only if the father was alive in 2005

questions.explanation: The right is by birth and the 2005 amendment has retroactive effect, so the father's survival is irrelevant.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under the Patents Act, 1970, the term of a patent is:

options.A: 14 years from the date of grant

questions.explanation: Section 53 provides a term of twenty years from the date of filing of the application.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: Under the Copyright Act, 1957, the term of copyright in a published literary work is:

options.A: The lifetime of the author plus 60 years
options.B: The lifetime of the author plus 50 years
options.D: 25 years from the date of creation

questions.explanation: Section 22 gives the author's lifetime plus sixty years, counted from the beginning of the year following death.

questions.subject: Intellectual Property Law
questions.question: A registered trade mark in India is valid initially for:
questions.explanation: Under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, registration lasts ten years and can be renewed indefinitely.

questions.subject: Environmental Law
questions.question: The National Green Tribunal was established under the:

options.C: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974

questions.explanation: The NGT handles disputes on environmental matters under the Act's seven scheduled statutes.

questions.subject: Environmental Law
questions.question: The 'polluter pays' principle was applied in India in:

options.A: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar
options.B: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P.
options.C: T.N. Godavarman v. Union of India
options.D: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India

questions.explanation: In the Bichhri (Rajasthan) case, the Court held polluters liable to bear the cost of remedial measures.

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question: Separate legal personality of a company was established by:

options.C: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.

questions.explanation: The House of Lords held the company a distinct person from its shareholders (1897).

questions.subject: Company Law
questions.question: The minimum number of members required to form a public company under the Companies Act, 2013 is:
questions.explanation: A private company needs at least two members; a public company needs at least seven.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: The maxim 'audi alteram partem' requires that:

options.A: Appeals must be allowed in every case
options.B: No one should be condemned unheard
options.C: No one should be a judge in his own cause

questions.explanation: It is the rule of fair hearing, a pillar of natural justice.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.question: The rule against bias is expressed in the maxim:
questions.explanation: No person shall be a judge in his own cause.

questions.subject: Information Technology Law
questions.question: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 was struck down in:

options.A: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
options.B: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)
options.D: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (1997)

questions.explanation: The Court held Section 66A violated Article 19(1)(a) and was not saved by Article 19(2).

questions.subject: Labour Law
questions.question: The 'triple test' for determining whether an establishment is an 'industry' was laid down in:

options.A: State of Bombay v. Hospital Mazdoor Sabha
options.B: Bangalore Water Supply Board v. A. Rajappa
options.C: Management of Safdarjung Hospital v. Kuldip Singh
options.D: Hussainbhai v. Alath Factory Employees Union

questions.explanation: The test looks at systematic activity, cooperation between employer and employee, and production or distribution of goods and services.

questions.subject: Women and Law
questions.question: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 was preceded by guidelines laid down in:

options.A: Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India
options.B: Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra

questions.explanation: Vishaka (1997) laid down binding guidelines using international conventions such as CEDAW.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.question: The principle that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once is protected by:
questions.explanation: Article 20(2) embodies the rule against double jeopardy; Article 20(1) bars ex post facto penal laws; Article 20(3) protects against self-incrimination.

questions.subject: Consumer Law
questions.question: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) and provisions on product liability were introduced by the:
questions.explanation: The 2019 Act replaced the 1986 Act and created the CCPA to regulate unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements.
